Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. C001069.text: This week marks four years since the tragic death of Sergeant First Class Michael Clark, a U.S. Army reservist from Bolton, CT, who diligently served his country with distinction. Today, Sgt. Clark’s legacy protects the families of fallen reservists service members from abruptly losing health care coverage. Soon after Michael Clark’s death during a training mission in 2022, his family was notified that the cost of their TRICARE health care coverage would sharply increase just six months after his passing – all because of an indefensible gap in our laws, that treated reservists either service connected fatality differently than active duty members. In 2023, I worked with the Clark family to introduce the Sergeant First Class Michael Clark TRICARE Reserve Parity Act. The bill was signed into law later that year, extending that six-month coverage window to three years. The Clark family’s experience exposed an injustice in the law that never should have existed. Thanks to their advocacy, the law now ensures full parity for guard and reserve survivor benefits that of active-duty personnel.

C000880.text: RT by @MikeCrapo: Senate Resolution with @SenJohnCurtis and @MikeCrapo in honor of Pioneer Day and the 179th anniversary of the Latter-day Saints entering the Salt Lake Valley: Recognizing the 179th anniversary of the arrival of pioneers belonging to The Church of Jesus Christ of Latterday Saints to the Great Salt Lake Valley, honoring the enduring pioneer spirit that shaped the American West, and celebrating its continued relevance to the unfolding American story. Whereas the early members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (referred to in this preamble as the ‘‘Church’’) sought nothing more than the freedom to worship according to the dictates of their own conscience; Whereas, in the years following the establishment of the Church, the early members of the Church endured repeated persecution, including mob violence, the destruction of their homes and crops, the loss of their property, and forced displacement from one settlement after another; Whereas, on June 27, 1844, Joseph Smith, the leader and prophet of the Church, was murdered by an armed mob, leaving the Church and its members facing an uncertain future; Whereas Brigham Young, who succeeded Joseph Smith as leader of the Church, concluded that safety and religious liberty could only be found far beyond the settled United States and organized the Church’s members for a journey into the wilderness of the American West; Whereas, beginning in February 1846, thousands of Latterday Saint pioneers set out across the frozen Iowa plains and ultimately traveled more than 1,300 miles by wagon and, for many, by foot, crossing prairies, deserts, mountains, and rivers to reach their new home; Whereas the Latter-day Saint pioneers endured extreme cold, disease, hunger, and exhaustion during the journey, and many families buried children, parents, and spouses along the trail, their graves marking a path of sacrifice across the American West; Whereas, upon entering the Great Salt Lake Valley on July 24, 1847, Brigham Young declared, ‘‘This is the right place,’’ foretelling how the valley would become home to many Latter-day Saint pioneers and their posterity; Whereas, within days of their arrival, the Latter-day Saint pioneers laid out a city, plowed fields, irrigated the desert, and began to build homes, mills, and churches where none had stood before; Whereas, over the following decades, tens of thousands more Latter-day Saint pioneers followed the same trail, and, together with earlier arrivals, established more than 500 communities throughout the American West, transforming the region into a place of prosperity; Whereas the industry of the Latter-day Saint pioneers extended far beyond their own settlements, as they built roads and bridges, operated ferries across major rivers, planted way-station crops, and assisted thousands of other westward-bound emigrants who relied on the resources and goodwill the Latter-day Saint pioneers had established; Whereas, on July 24, 1849, the Latter-day Saint pioneers held their first formal commemoration of the anniversary of their arrival, gathering for a procession and a public celebration of thanksgiving in Salt Lake City; Whereas that observance has continued for 177 years and is now celebrated annually as ‘‘Pioneer Day,’’ a Utah State holiday marked by parades, rodeos, reenactments, fireworks, and civic gatherings that welcome participants of every faith and background; Whereas the story of the Latter-day Saint pioneers is, at its core, a distinctly American story of a people who, having been denied protection and refuge, built both for themselves and for the generations who followed; Whereas the pioneer spirit of self-reliance, enterprise, and perseverance that carried the Latter-day Saint pioneers across the plains continues today in the character of the American West, which remains a place where individuals and communities join together to solve hard problems and build for the future; I voted for the National Defense Authorization Act because I have always believed that it is our responsibility to provide our men and women in uniform with the resources they need to defend our nation and take care of their families. This bill makes important investments in our service members by improving military pay, strengthening housing, expanding access to childcare, and providing additional support for school districts that serve military families. These are commonsense investments that recognize the sacrifices our troops and their loved ones make every day. Furthermore, it builds on pre-existing cooperation with our allies and does not merge militaries with anyone. It also ensures continued oversight and accountability. This House vote on the NDAA is one step in the legislative process—not the final product. I will continue working with Republicans and Democrats to produce a final bipartisan bill that strengthens our national security, supports our troops and military families, and reflects Congress' responsibility to carefully oversee matters of war and peace. At the same time, I remain committed to Congress' constitutional role in decisions regarding the use of military force. Senate Resolution with @SenJohnCurtis and @MikeCrapo in honor of Pioneer Day and the 179th anniversary of the Latter-day Saints entering the Salt Lake Valley: Recognizing the 179th anniversary of the arrival of pioneers belonging to The Church of Jesus Christ of Latterday Saints to the Great Salt Lake Valley, honoring the enduring pioneer spirit that shaped the American West, and celebrating its continued relevance to the unfolding American story. Whereas the early members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (referred to in this preamble as the ‘‘Church’’) sought nothing more than the freedom to worship according to the dictates of their own conscience; Whereas, in the years following the establishment of the Church, the early members of the Church endured repeated persecution, including mob violence, the destruction of their homes and crops, the loss of their property, and forced displacement from one settlement after another; Whereas, on June 27, 1844, Joseph Smith, the leader and prophet of the Church, was murdered by an armed mob, leaving the Church and its members facing an uncertain future; Whereas Brigham Young, who succeeded Joseph Smith as leader of the Church, concluded that safety and religious liberty could only be found far beyond the settled United States and organized the Church’s members for a journey into the wilderness of the American West; Whereas, beginning in February 1846, thousands of Latterday Saint pioneers set out across the frozen Iowa plains and ultimately traveled more than 1,300 miles by wagon and, for many, by foot, crossing prairies, deserts, mountains, and rivers to reach their new home; Whereas the Latter-day Saint pioneers endured extreme cold, disease, hunger, and exhaustion during the journey, and many families buried children, parents, and spouses along the trail, their graves marking a path of sacrifice across the American West; Whereas, upon entering the Great Salt Lake Valley on July 24, 1847, Brigham Young declared, ‘‘This is the right place,’’ foretelling how the valley would become home to many Latter-day Saint pioneers and their posterity; Whereas, within days of their arrival, the Latter-day Saint pioneers laid out a city, plowed fields, irrigated the desert, and began to build homes, mills, and churches where none had stood before; Whereas, over the following decades, tens of thousands more Latter-day Saint pioneers followed the same trail, and, together with earlier arrivals, established more than 500 communities throughout the American West, transforming the region into a place of prosperity; Whereas the industry of the Latter-day Saint pioneers extended far beyond their own settlements, as they built roads and bridges, operated ferries across major rivers, planted way-station crops, and assisted thousands of other westward-bound emigrants who relied on the resources and goodwill the Latter-day Saint pioneers had established; Whereas, on July 24, 1849, the Latter-day Saint pioneers held their first formal commemoration of the anniversary of their arrival, gathering for a procession and a public celebration of thanksgiving in Salt Lake City; Whereas that observance has continued for 177 years and is now celebrated annually as ‘‘Pioneer Day,’’ a Utah State holiday marked by parades, rodeos, reenactments, fireworks, and civic gatherings that welcome participants of every faith and background; Whereas the story of the Latter-day Saint pioneers is, at its core, a distinctly American story of a people who, having been denied protection and refuge, built both for themselves and for the generations who followed; Whereas the pioneer spirit of self-reliance, enterprise, and perseverance that carried the Latter-day Saint pioneers across the plains continues today in the character of the American West, which remains a place where individuals and communities join together to solve hard problems and build for the future; and (Continued below)

R to @SenMikeLee: Whereas the legacy of the Latter-day Saint pioneers stands as a lasting reminder that the American story is written not only by the founding generation, but by every generation that chooses to press forward with unconquerable faith and undaunted hope: Now, therefore, be it Resolved, That the Senate— (1) recognizes the 179th anniversary of the arrival of Latter-day Saint pioneers to the Great Salt Lake Valley on July 24, 1847, and the annual observance of ‘‘Pioneer Day’’ that commemorates it; (2) honors the extraordinary sacrifice of the Latter-day Saint pioneers, including those who gave their lives along the trail, in pursuit of religious liberty and a place to call home; (3) commends the Latter-day Saint pioneers and their descendants for their foundational role in settling and developing the American West, and for a legacy of industry, cooperation, and faith that continues to benefit the United States; and (4) encourages all the people of the United States to reflect on the enduring virtues of the Latter-day Saint pioneers and to carry forward, in their own generation, that same spirit of resilience in the continuation of the American story.

RT by @SenTedCruz: U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz is urging Congress to act on the future of college sports. In a @USATODAY op-ed, Cruz argues that without federal action, college football could become "a super league of just a handful of the wealthiest schools." MORE: https://ow.ly/SfCe50ZrUJj

College sports are on an unsustainable path. If Congress doesn't act, we lose the games we love to a super league of a handful of rich schools. My new op-ed in @USATODAY: For hundreds of thousands of student athletes, college sports are an opportunity. Sports are a means to a better life because they teach young men and women the traits that are necessary to succeed as adults – grit, work ethic, self-discipline and teamwork. Student athletes often must train before sunrise, balance full academic schedules and compete for their teammates, their schools and the communities that stand behind them. At a time when Americans are divided on so many issues, seeing young men and women mature through sports is one thing that unites and inspires us. College sports remain a rare tradition that still brings people together. On fall Saturdays during football season, college towns come alive. Stands fill with school colors, marching bands echo through the afternoon air, and thousands of families, friends and alumni return to campus, carrying decades of pride and history into every rivalry game. Yet the foundation that has sustained college athletics is beginning to crack. In fact, college sports are changing faster than ever. Schools are losing tens of millions of dollars attempting to keep up with an out-of-control spending arms race. Eligibility is being decided by lawsuits and injunctions, leaving local judges to rewrite the rules in favor of their hometown teams. Pro athletes are now trying to return to play in college, stealing roster spots from 18-year-old students. Sports that don't generate significant revenue, including many women’s sports and sports featured in Olympic competitions, are being canceled week after week. As Derek Mason, the head coach of Middle Tennessee State football, put it, college sports look like “The Hunger Games. COLLEGE SPORTS ARE ON AN UNSUSTAINABLE PATH If things don't change, we are headed toward a future where college athletics, and specifically college football, will be reduced to a super league of just a handful of the wealthiest schools. That’s a future in which America may lose its dominance in Olympic sports. A future in which hundreds of thousands of athletic scholarships disappear. This damage is already visible. In the past two years, more than 400 college sports programs have been canceled or gutted. USC, UCLA, Oregon and Washington joined the Big Ten, while Stanford and California went to the Atlantic Coast Conference, decimating the Pac-12, a conference with roots dating to 1915. These events have led to calls for Congress to step up. While some fans and pundits scoff at lawmakers’ involvement, the reality is the legal problems and court battles consuming college sports are the result of laws previously enacted by Congress. Only Congress can fix those laws so there is a clear and enforceable national rulebook for college sports. If lawmakers don't act, the college sports landscape that Americans have known for generations will soon cease to exist. As chairman of the U.S. Senate Commerce Committee, which has jurisdiction over college athletics, and as a Texan who understands that football is more than merely a pastime, I have spent the past three years working to craft a solution. Over the last several months, I spent countless hours at the negotiating table with my Democratic counterpart, U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state, searching for common ground. After hundreds of difficult conversations and hard-fought compromises, we produced the Protect College Sports Act – a bipartisan bill designed not only to address issues around name, image and likeness deals, but also to stabilize college athletics for future generations to come. RULES MUST BE UNIFORM AND FAIRLY APPLIED The act would end the chaos and solve the immediate crisis that has fans most alarmed. First and foremost, it would empower schools to set and enforce national rules around fair competition, recruiting and tampering so coaches could build and sustain their programs. It would prevent the formation of a super league that would throw away more than a century of tradition. It would create clear national rules for transfers and eligibility. Meaningful rules and stability will also ensure Olympic sports don't become casualties of the ongoing arms race. Perhaps as important, it would protect student athletes from unscrupulous agents, ensure they have access to medical care, protect scholarships for the injured, and create an independent ombudsman office to assist them in making sense of their new rights. Student athletes would have guaranteed opportunities to play and earn from their licensing deals, as well as getting their degrees. PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT HAS BROAD BIPARTISAN AND UNIVERSITY SUPPORT During committee discussion of the legislation, the bill was amended to address many stakeholder concerns, which led to an overwhelming bipartisan vote of more than two-thirds of committee members in support, propelling its advancement to the Senate floor. The bill has the backing of more than 260 universities and colleges, including hundreds of coaches, student athletes and key stakeholders like the President’s College Sports Commission. President Donald Trump supports our work on this issue and wants to see a bill on his desk “before it’s too late.” We cannot wait until the system completely collapses and then attempt to rebuild what was lost. College sports are one of America's great unifying traditions, and if we want to preserve them for future generations, the Senate and House of Representatives must act now.

F000466.text: Gerard “Jerry” Jonas of Levittown lived a remarkable American story—and everywhere that story took him, Jerry served. He served his country first. As a United States Marine during the Korean War, he served in combat and earned a battlefield promotion to sergeant. Like so many of his generation, he came home, took off the uniform, and went to work building a better future for his family, community, and the country he loved. He built that future in Levittown, where he and his beloved Betty raised six children and made their home in Cobalt Ridge a place of faith, laughter, loyalty, and love. He built it at Queen of the Universe Parish, where he was an original parishioner, coach, volunteer, fundraiser, writer, and steady presence—living his faith not only in words, but in daily acts of responsibility and service. He built it with his remarkable gift for communication: first helping tell the story of America’s early space and missile programs as a technical writer and editor, then bringing that same curiosity and craftsmanship to advertising, sports promotion, and more than 30 years of beloved columns in the Bucks County Courier Times. For decades, Jerry helped give Lower Bucks County a voice. He captured its humor, its memory, its people, its pride, and its heart. And even in retirement, he kept serving. Through Operation Stand Down, Jerry stood with fellow veterans and helped men and women who had worn the uniform find dignity, support, and a path forward. That is why Jerry Jonas was a true Bucks County legend. He served his country. He loved his family. He lived his faith. He told our stories. He advocated for our veterans. And he truly left his corner of the world better than he found it. Please join me in extending prayers to Jerry’s family, friends, and all who loved him, and may we honor his extraordinary life by carrying forward the same faith, patriotism, good humor, loyalty, and servant’s heart that made Jerry Jonas such a gift to Levittown and all of Bucks County.

Fun Fact Friday: As we celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, I want to highlight some of the signers of the Declaration of Independence. Francis Lewis was born in Wales in 1713. Orphaned at age 5, he went to live with his extended family. At age 21, he converted land he had inherited from his father into merchandise, and moved to New York City. During the French and Indian War, he worked supplying uniforms to the British military. While working as a clothing contractor, the fort he was operating out of was attacked, and he was taken prisoner in France. Upon being released in a prisoner exchange, the British government granted him 5,000 acres of land in New York as compensation. Taxation without Representation hit Lewis hard, and he became an advocate to break away from the British government. Lewis was a founding member of the Sons of Liberty, was elected to the Continental Congress, and financially supported the war for independence. Lewis signed the Declaration on August 2, 1776.
